title: How the AP Decides Who Won an Election
summary: On election night, news that a candidate has won often comes from The Associated Press, or AP. The AP has tracked United States elections for 178 years. It will count results for nearly 7,000 races, including Congress and governor races. About 4,000 journalists will collect results, and around 1,000 clerks will enter the totals. Then the AP's Decision Team studies the results. A race is not called until the other candidates have no path left to win. Certainty is the standard, said David Scott, the AP's vice president for U.S. election services. In 1972, about 95 percent voted in person on Election Day, but now less than half do, and most vote early, by mail or in person. The AP is also working with news networks on a new Voter Poll. It cannot call a race, but it can show which way an election may be going. Some races take longer. The AP called the 2020 presidential election four days later. In 2000, it never called the race between George W. Bush and Al Gore because Florida was too close.
why_it_matters: When you hear who won on election night, knowing someone checked the numbers carefully helps you trust that the winner was really chosen by the voters.

background_read: The Associated Press collects and studies election results from races across the country.
A race is only called when the other candidates have no path left to win, so the winner must be certain.
Waiting for that certainty helps make sure the winner is announced correctly, even if some races take longer to decide.

WHAT: The AP collects vote totals, studies the results, and calls a winner only when the result is certain
WHERE: Across the United States, in races including Congress and governor races
WHY: So that a winner is announced only when the other candidates have no path left to win
